title: Week in Review: Emanuel ‘Chris’ Welch on Veto Session Priorities, Ending His Speakership
summary: Week in Review: Emanuel ‘Chris’ Welch on Veto Session Priorities, Ending His Speakership Jessica Watts Fri, 11/27/2026 - 17:30 Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch (D-Westchester) was first elected to the House in 2012 and was chosen as speaker in January 2021. Earlier this month, he announced he’ll continue to serve as state representative for the House’s 7th District, but won’t seek a fourth term as leader. Welch faced criticism over how his office handled sexual harassment complaints against former state Rep. Harry Benton (D-Plainfield). Several Democrats have already announced their candidacy to succeed Welch. Lawmakers are due back in Springfield next week for the second week of veto session, with pressure to pass legislation that would keep the Chicago Bears in Illinois, regulate data centers and set aside more state money to fund public schools. Welch joined a special edition of “Week in Review” to discuss his priorities for the rest of the veto session, reflect on his time as speaker and more. On data center regulation: “What we heard at the doors, regularly, no matter what part of the state you lived in, was people wanting something to be done about data centers. And so, that’s a top priority for us. Negotiations are ongoing. That’s another group of folks sitting around a table pretty regularly. I just got an update yesterday. You have labor at the table, you have environmental groups at the table, the House, the Senate, the governor’s office. Everyone’s at the table. And as long as we’re at the table and the conversations are still happening, there’s a possibility that we can get something done.” On funding public schools: “All of us always want to do more for our schools. All across the state, whether you’re in Chicago, whether you’re in Proviso Township like myself, or the Metro East, we all want to do more for our schools. The question is how do you do it with limited resources? Where do you find the resources to get it done? And that’s been our issue. And I certainly hope that we continue that conversation, this is a very important conversation. … I think if we can better fund our local schools, better fund the (evidence)-based funding formula, school districts don’t have to raise their property taxes as high as they have been. And so I do think the state plays a role in that and I think we can do better.” On why he decided not to seek a fourth term as House speaker: “I’ve always believed that our time in these positions is finite, but the work that we do is infinite. You always know that your time is gonna come up and you hope that while you’re there that you can leave the place better than how you found it. I think that my six years as speaker has truly been the honor of a lifetime. I’ve served in a historic speakership for our state as the first Black lawmaker who’s ever done it. But I knew the time was gonna come to an end.” On his alleged mishandling of sexual harassment cases: Despite initially being made aware of complaints against Benton in 2023, Welch did not call for Benton’s resignation until earlier this year, following a report by the legislative inspector general that concluded Benton committed two acts of sexual harassment. “Hindsight is 20/20, it’s perfect vision as they say. There’s some things that I would’ve done differently today. And I think it’s extremely important to acknowledge that. But I do wanna say, at the time, I took the advice of multiple counsel (and) respected the survivor’s wishes, but when I look back on it, certainly there are some things that I would do differently.” On other controversies: The Chicago Sun Times reported on an alleged domestic violence incident in 2002 that generated a police report but no charges. The article mentioned lawsuits alleging harassment and retaliation during Welch’s time on the Proviso Township High School Board of Education, but those suits were later dropped. Welch also faced criticism for his interactions with a former staffer; he has since apologized . Twenty-six state representatives in the House Democratic Caucus signed a letter opposing another term of Welch as House speaker. “Those issues have been raised every two years that I’ve been in elected office for the past 25+ years. They’ve been in every campaign, they were part of the speaker campaign in 2021. … I’ve always answered questions regarding all of those matters. I’ve always been open and accessible and transparent about any of those things. I’ve never tried to hide anything. And I’m going to continue to be that way. I’m going to continue to be my authentic self. And if anyone has a question about anything, I’ve always said, ‘I’m accessible, come talk to me.’” On the qualities lawmakers should look for in the next House speaker: “The voters have sent a very powerful message in electing the largest Democratic majority in modern history. Eighty-four (Democrats) will be the caucus that the new speaker inherits. No speaker has ever led 84 in this modern era. And we need someone that’s gonna unite the caucus and accept that mandate that the voters have just given us. They want us to deliver on the affordability issues that they’re all suffering from. They don’t want us fighting each other. And I think that’s extremely important and that’s why I made the decision that I made, and when I made it.” On whether the SAFE-T Act should be amended: “The SAFE-T Act is good policy. It’s policy that’s working. What we have seen the last couple years is record-low numbers when it comes to murders in the city of Chicago. The crime rate is down year over year the last couple of years and that’s because the SAFE-T Act is working. Are there ways of making things better? I’d love to hear ‘em. The General Assembly would love to hear those ways.” On his proudest achievement as House speaker: “We’ve accomplished some great things, from the Clean and Equitable Jobs Act, landmark energy legislation, a ban on assault weapons, transit reform, … Karina’s Law, taking weapons out of the hands of abusers, the list goes on. We’ve had major policy victories under my leadership as speaker.” On his biggest disappointment as House Speaker: “My biggest disappointment, honestly, is the Benton situation. I think this has left an amazing stain on what was really a good speakership and I certainly wish we could’ve done things better.” The Week in Review
